title: List of Forms and Contact Details Required to Request Medical Records From Mount Sinai Health System in 2026
summary: Find the exact forms, addresses, and phone numbers needed to request medical records from Mount Sinai Health System in 2026, plus how PI firms avoid authorization rejections and get complete records in a couple of weeks.
body_markdown:
Requesting medical records from Mount Sinai Health System means knowing which form to use, where to send it, and how to sidestep the small mistakes that stall a request for weeks. For personal injury attorneys, that gets complicated fast across seven hospital campuses and more than 400 outpatient practices. Routing varies by facility, some locations share Health Information Management contact information, and Mount Sinai Doctors practices may use practice-specific or online pathways. Firms that want to stop managing this by hand often turn to[Codes Health](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) for AI-powered retrieval that works toward complete records in a couple of weeks rather than months, with authorization validation and persistent follow-up built in.


## **Key Takeaways**


-


Mount Sinai uses two primary authorization forms: MR-200 for patient self-requests and MR-201 for third-party requests, including attorneys


-


All forms are available in[six languages](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/medical-records) : English, Arabic, Greek, Russian, Spanish, and Simplified Chinese


-


Mount Sinai says it generally responds to completed requests within[7 to 10 days](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/medical-records) , and its published policy also references HIPAA's 30-day access timeframe


-


Three facilities do not accept in-person requests: Mount Sinai Beth Israel, Mount Sinai-Union Square, and Mount Sinai-Behavioral Health Center


-


Mount Sinai says parties such as attorneys, insurers, and subpoena requesters may be charged[$0.75 per page](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/medical-records) , while patients may be charged $6.50 for records delivered electronically


-


Mount Sinai's current sources publish conflicting contact details for the Queens mailing address and the Chelsea records phone number, so call to confirm before you send anything


-


Codes Health uses AI-assisted validation to catch authorization errors before submission, heading off the rejections that force a corrected resubmission


## **Understanding the Mount Sinai Medical Records Request Process**


### **General Overview of Requesting Records**


Mount Sinai Health System runs one of the largest healthcare networks in New York City, with[hospitals and outpatient practices](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/facts) across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and Long Island. Health Information Management departments process record requests, though several locations share the same address and phone number.


There are three submission methods: online portal access through MyMountSinai for patients, mail or fax submission using official authorization forms, and in-person requests at facilities that accept walk-ins.


For legal professionals, the third-party pathway requires Form MR-201, which designates the authorized recipient and specifies the records needed. The patient or their legal representative has to sign it.


### **Key Steps for Initiating a Request**


Before submitting anything, gather the patient's full legal name and date of birth, the medical record number if you have it, the specific dates of service, the names of treating physicians or departments, and a clear description of the records needed, whether medical, billing, or imaging. Incomplete information can cause record-request rejections or delays.


## **Navigating Mount Sinai's Online Portal for Medical Records**


### **Accessing Records via MyMountSinai**


The MyMountSinai patient portal gives patients digital access to test results, visit summaries, and treatment notes across Mount Sinai facilities.


Some records requested through MyMountSinai may be available immediately. Mount Sinai's Sharing Hub offers snapshot and formal-copy options, and Mount Sinai says it generally responds to non-immediate record requests within 7 to 10 business days.


Mount Sinai South Nassau currently continues to offer FollowMyHealth for patients accessing certain[personal medical records](https://www.mountsinai.org/locations/south-nassau/visit/medical-records) . Its website also provides access to MyMountSinai.


### **Benefits of Online Record Access**


For patients handling their own records, portal access is the fastest route. Attorneys requesting records directly from Mount Sinai should use the third-party authorization process rather than relying on the patient's portal, which means Form MR-201 even when the client has an active MyMountSinai account.


For Mount Sinai Doctors offices, Mount Sinai offers a separate online records-request tool hosted through Swellbox, and some requests may need to go to the practice directly.


## **Essential Forms for Releasing Mount Sinai Medical Records**


### **Key Sections of a Release Form**


Mount Sinai requires authorization forms that comply with[HIPAA Privacy Rule](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/compliance/hipaa-privacy-security-compliance-program) requirements. The two primary forms:


**Form MR-200: Patient Access Request**


-


Used when patients request their own records


-


Requires patient signature and date


-


Must specify records requested and date ranges


-


Available in six languages


**Form MR-201: Third Party Authorization**


-


Required for attorneys, insurance companies, and other third parties


-


Must include designation of authorized recipient


-


Requires include or do-not-include selections for sensitive record categories


-


States that the authorization is valid for one year from the date signed unless another expiration date or event is specified


Both forms address sensitive categories, which the current MR-201 identifies as:


-


HIV-related information


-


Alcohol and drug abuse records


-


Psychiatric records


-


Genetic testing results


Complete the include and do-not-include selections for these categories carefully. Incomplete or ambiguous authorization may prevent Mount Sinai from releasing the requested sensitive information.


### **Where to Obtain Official Release Forms**


All forms can be downloaded from the[Mount Sinai medical records](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/medical-records) page in PDF, in all six languages.

## **How to Obtain Old Medical Records From Mount Sinai**


### **Specific Procedures for Archived Records**


Mount Sinai says it maintains records for a[minimum of 10 years](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/medical-records) after the last visit, with pediatric records retained until the patient reaches age 21. That is Mount Sinai's own policy, not a universal New York minimum; New York's general rule for physician offices can be shorter, at six years after the last visit and one year after a minor turns 18.


Archived records use the same forms but may take longer. Mount Sinai notes that older records may require additional time because some are stored outside the hospital.


### **Challenges With Older Records**


Legacy records from facilities Mount Sinai acquired over the years may sit in different systems, filed under a previous facility name or numbering scheme. When you request older records, include as much identifying detail as you can: previous facility names, approximate treatment dates, treating physicians, and the department or specialty involved.


For cases spanning multiple years and facilities, firms often find a specialized retrieval service can locate and compile records faster than filing separate requests one facility at a time.

### **Physical Address for Mail-In Requests**


Mail requests to the Health Information Management department at the facility where treatment occurred, with the completed MR-200 or MR-201. On identification, Mount Sinai requires a valid government-issued photo ID for in-person requests, and South Nassau separately instructs patients who mail its form to include a copy of ID. Check the facility's instructions before mailing.


Mount Sinai's system-level instructions identify[medicalrecordrequests@mountsinai.org](https://www.mountsinai.org/locations/south-nassau/visit/medical-records) for South Nassau only. Other hospitals on the central records page are directed to the listed mail and in-person pathways, while Mount Sinai Doctors practices may have their own procedures.

## **Ensuring Completeness and Accuracy of Mount Sinai Records**


### **Checking for Gaps in Retrieved Records**


Getting records back is not the same as getting complete records. Check delivered material against the original request before you close out the retrieval. Common gaps include:


-


Missing billing records when only medical records were delivered


-


Absent imaging reports or radiology results


-


Incomplete date ranges


-


Missing records from affiliated facilities


### **Resolving Discrepancies With Mount Sinai**


When records look incomplete, contact the Health Information Management department at that facility, reference your original request date, and name exactly which records are missing. Mount Sinai's[HIPAA compliance program](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/compliance/hipaa-privacy-security-compliance-program) governs how facilities handle requests, though follow-up often takes several contacts.


Codes Health handles this through its completeness review, checking delivered records against the original request before returning materials to the firm and working with the facility to resolve any gaps before closing the retrieval.


## **HIPAA Authorization for Family Members and Third-Party Access**


### **Requirements for Family Access**


Whether a family member can obtain records depends on the patient's status, that person's legal authority, and applicable state and federal law. HIPAA and New York law distinguish among personal representatives, parents, guardians, health-care agents, executors, administrators, and distributees.


-


**For minors** : a parent or legal guardian generally may request records when legally authorized to act for the child, subject to exceptions for certain confidential services and other circumstances governed by state and federal law


-


**For incapacitated adults** : a health care proxy or court-appointed guardianship papers may establish authority


-


**For deceased patients** : Mount Sinai may permit an established next of kin, executor, or court-appointed administrator to request records. If the patient did not die at a Mount Sinai facility, Mount Sinai says a death certificate is required to verify death. Additional proof of legal authority may be required depending on the requester's status


The authorization should clearly identify the relationship and the legal basis for access.


### **Authorizing Legal Representatives**


Attorneys submit Form MR-201 with the patient's signature (or a legal representative's signature with supporting documentation), clear identification of the firm as authorized recipient, specific records and date ranges, and include or do-not-include selections for any sensitive categories.


On powers of attorney, the New York State Department of Health states that an attorney representing a qualified person needs a signed power of attorney authorizing the attorney to request medical records. Health-care agents and other personal representatives may have access within the scope of authority granted by applicable law.


## **Avoiding Delays in Mount Sinai Record Retrieval**


### **Common Causes of Delays**


Authorization errors are a common cause of record-request rejections and delays. The issues that come up most:


-


Missing patient signature


-


Missing or invalid authorization dates, including an undated patient signature


-


Incomplete sensitive-record selections when psychiatric or alcohol and drug abuse records are needed


-


Incorrect facility address routing the request to the wrong department


-


Blurry or expired photo ID copies


-


Incomplete date ranges leaving gaps in requested records


A rejected or incomplete authorization can require correction and resubmission, causing additional delay.


### **Best Practices for Faster Retrieval**


Before submitting, verify:


-


Correct form selected, MR-200 or MR-201


-


Patient signature present and dated, and all required fields completed


-


Expiration date or event entered if you need something other than the default one-year term


-


Sensitive-record selections completed if applicable


-


Legible photo ID attached where the facility requires it


-


Correct facility address and specific date ranges


Incomplete authorizations are a leading cause of denied requests. Missing patient signatures, unclear expiration dates, or unchecked boxes for sensitive records can force a corrected resubmission and push your timeline out. Under the federal HIPAA right of access, covered entities generally must act on a request within 30 days, with state law sometimes setting different requirements. ## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What is the typical timeframe for Mount Sinai to process a records request?**


Mount Sinai says it generally responds to completed requests within 7 to 10 business days, although its published policy also references HIPAA's 30-day access timeframe. Under New York Public Health Law §18, qualified persons generally must be given an opportunity to inspect records within 10 days of a written request; separate rules govern requested copies, and the law does not impose a universal 10-day delivery deadline. Archived records or multi-facility requests may take longer.


### **Is there a fee to request medical records from Mount Sinai?**


Mount Sinai states that it may charge patients $6.50 for records delivered electronically. If fees apply, paper delivery of electronic records is $0.07 per page, and paper copies of original paper records are $0.12 per page. For other parties such as attorneys, insurance companies, and subpoena requests, Mount Sinai says a fee of up to $0.75 per page may be charged. Mount Sinai says it does not charge for urgent in-person requests or for records submitted to physicians or other health care providers.


### **What should I do if my request is denied or delayed?**


Start with the Health Information Management department at that facility to find the specific reason, usually an incomplete form, a missing signature, or an unclear date range. If you believe your rights under HIPAA or New York law have been violated, Mount Sinai's[Privacy Office](https://www.mountsinai.org/about/compliance/hipaa-privacy-security-compliance-program) can be reached at 212-241-3211. Depending on the issue, complaints may also go to the HHS Office for Civil Rights or the New York State Department of Health.


### **Can I request imaging studies like X-rays and MRIs?**


Yes. X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and radiology reports can be requested using the same authorization forms; specify the imaging type and dates. Imaging may be provided on CD or electronically depending on the facility and file size. For NY Eye and Ear Infirmary record requests, including those involving imaging, the published Medical Records number is 212-979-4352.


### **How do I request records for a patient who has passed away?**


Mount Sinai may permit an established next of kin, executor, or court-appointed administrator to request records. If the patient did not die at a Mount Sinai facility, Mount Sinai says a death certificate is required to verify death. Additional proof of legal authority may be required depending on the requester's status, and New York law can also recognize distributees where there is no will. Contact the facility's Health Information Management department for guidance on its specific procedures.
